<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Canadian Securitization Program</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Prior
to termination, the Company had a $70 million Canadian (approximately $57
million U.S. as of December&nbsp;31, 2008) accounts receivable securitization
program, whereby the Company sold, without recourse, on an ongoing basis,
certain of its Canadian accounts receivable to a trust in which the Company
held a variable interest, but was not the primary beneficiary.&#160; Accordingly, under ASC 810, &#147;Consolidation,&#148;
accounts receivable sold to the trust, for which the Company was not the
primary beneficiary, were not included in the accompanying consolidated balance
sheets.&#160; The Company had retained
servicing responsibilities and a subordinated interest in future cash flows
from the receivables.&#160; The Company
received rights to future cash flows arising after the investors in the
securitization trust had received the return for which they had contracted.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The
Company&#146;s residual interest in the securitization program was recorded at fair
value and was based upon the total outstanding receivables sold, adjusted for
dilution and loss reserves of approximately 4.0% at December&nbsp;31, 2008 less
the amount funded to the Company.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">At
December&nbsp;31, 2008, $58 million of accounts receivable had been sold under
the program, of which $23 million were retained by the Company as a subordinated
interest.&#160; The amount funded to the
Company at December&nbsp;31, 2008 was $33 million.&#160; The Company&#146;s retained interest was included
in retained interest in receivables sold in the accompanying consolidated
balance sheet at December&nbsp;31, 2008.&#160;
The Company recognized a loss on sales of receivables to the trust of $3
million in 2008 which was included in other, net in the consolidated statements
of operations.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Timberland Sale and Note Monetization</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The
Company sold approximately 980,000 acres of owned and leased timberland in
Florida, Georgia and Alabama in October&nbsp;1999.&#160; The final purchase price, after adjustments,
was $710 million.&#160; The Company received
$225 million in cash, with the balance of $485 million in the form of
installment notes.&#160; The Company entered
into a program to monetize the installment notes receivable.&#160; The notes were sold without recourse to
Timber Note Holdings LLC (&#147;TNH&#148;), a qualified special-purpose entity under the
provisions of ASC 860, for $430 million cash proceeds and a residual interest
in the notes.&#160; The transaction was
accounted for as a sale under ASC 860.&#160;
The cash proceeds from the sale and monetization transactions were used
to prepay borrowings under the Company&#146;s Credit Agreement.&#160; The residual interest was $36 million and $34
million at December&nbsp;31, 2009 and 2008, respectively, and is included in
other assets in the accompanying consolidated balance sheets.&#160; Cash flows received on the Company&#146;s retained
interest in TNH were $1 million and $13 million in 2009 and 2008,
respectively.&#160; The key economic
assumption used in measuring the residual interest at the date of monetization
was the rate at which the residual cash flows were discounted (9%).&#160; At December&nbsp;31, 2009, the sensitivity on
the current fair value of the residual cash flows to immediate 10% and 20%
adverse changes in the assumed rate at which the residual cash flows were
discounted (9%) was an insignificant amount and $1 million, respectively.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">70<a name="PB_70_120020_8146"></a></font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Bank Credit Facilities</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company and its
subsidiary, SSC Canada, as borrowers, and SSCC, as guarantor, entered into a
credit agreement, as amended (the &#147;Credit Agreement&#148;) on November&nbsp;1,
2004.&#160; The Credit Agreement provided for (i)&nbsp;a
revolving credit facility of $600 million to the Company (&#147;U.S. Revolver&#148;), of
which $512 million was borrowed as of December&nbsp;31, 2009 and (ii)&nbsp;a
revolving credit facility of $200 million to the Company and SSC Canada (&#147;SSC
Canada Revolver&#148;), of which $198 million was borrowed as of December&nbsp;31,
2009.&#160; Each of these revolving credit
facilities matured on November&nbsp;1, 2009.&#160;
The Credit Agreement provided for a Tranche B term loan to the Company
in the aggregate principal amount of $975 million, with an outstanding balance
of $137 million at December&nbsp;31, 2009.&#160;&#160;
The Credit Agreement also provided to SSC Canada a Tranche C term loan
in the aggregate principal amount of $300 million and a Tranche C-1 term loan
in the aggregate principal amount of $90 million, with outstanding balances of
$258 million and $78 million, respectively, at December&nbsp;31, 2009.&#160; The term loans are payable in quarterly
installments and mature on November&nbsp;1, 2011.&#160; The Company has the option to borrow at a
rate equal to LIBOR plus 2.25% or ABR plus 1.25% for the term loan facilities
and LIBOR plus 2.50% or ABR plus 1.50% for the revolving credit facilities (the
&#147;Applicable Rate&#148;).</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The
obligations of the Company under the Credit Agreement are unconditionally
guaranteed by SSCC and the material U.S. subsidiaries of the Company.&#160; The obligations of SSC Canada under the
Credit Agreement are unconditionally guaranteed by SSCC, the Company, the
material U.S. subsidiaries of the Company and the material Canadian
subsidiaries of SSC Canada.&#160; The
obligations of the Company under the Credit Agreement are secured by a security
interest in substantially all of the assets and properties of SSCC, the Company
and the material U.S. subsidiaries of the Company, by a pledge of all of the
capital stock of the Company and the material U.S. subsidiaries of the Company
and by a pledge of 65% of the capital stock of SSC Canada that is directly
owned by the Company.&#160; The security
interests securing the Company&#146;s obligation under the Credit Agreement exclude
cash, cash equivalents, certain trade receivables and the land and buildings of
certain corrugated container facilities.&#160;
The obligations of SSC Canada under the Credit Agreement are secured by
a security interest in substantially all of the assets and properties of SSC
Canada and the material Canadian subsidiaries of SSC Canada, by a pledge of all
of the capital stock of the material Canadian subsidiaries of SSC Canada and by
the same U.S. assets, properties and capital stock that secure the Company&#146;s obligations
under the Credit Agreement.&#160; The security
interests securing SSC Canada&#146;s obligation under the Credit Agreement exclude
certain other real property located in New Brunswick and Quebec.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The
Credit Agreement contains various covenants and restrictions including (i)&nbsp;limitations
on dividends, redemptions and repurchases of capital stock, (ii)&nbsp;limitations
on the incurrence of indebtedness, liens, leases and sale-leaseback
transactions, (iii)&nbsp;limitations on capital expenditures and (iv)&nbsp;maintenance
of certain financial covenants.&#160; The
Credit Agreement also requires prepayments if the Company has excess cash
flows, as defined, or receives proceeds from certain asset sales, insurance or
incurrence of certain indebtedness.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">As
of December&nbsp;31, 2009, as a result of the Company&#146;s default, the Company
had no availability for borrowings under the Company&#146;s revolving credit
facilities, after giving consideration to outstanding letters of credit of $87
million. &#160;As of December&nbsp;31, 2009, the Company had
available unrestricted cash and cash equivalents of $704 million primarily
invested in money market funds at a variable interest rate of 0.13%.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">During
the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2009, letters of credit in the amount of $71
million were drawn on to fund obligations principally related to non-qualified
pension plans, commodity derivative instruments and a guarantee for a
previously non-consolidated affiliate, which increased borrowings under the
Company&#146;s U.S. Revolver and SSC Canada Revolver by $44 million and $27 million,
respectively.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The
Company&#146;s Credit Agreement provided for a deposit funded letter of credit
facility, related to the variable rate industrial revenue bonds, for
approximately $122 million that was due to mature on November&nbsp;1,
2010.&#160; In February&nbsp;2009, due to an
event of default under the bond indentures, this credit facility was drawn on
to fully repay the industrial revenue bonds in the aggregate principal amount

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">DIP Credit Agreement</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In connection with filing the Chapter 11 Petition and the Canadian
Petition, on January&nbsp;26, 2009 the Company, SSCC and certain of its
affiliates filed a motion with the Bankruptcy Courts seeking approval to enter
into a DIP Credit Agreement.&#160; Final
approval of the DIP Credit Agreement was granted by the U.S. Court on February&nbsp;23,
2009 and by the Canadian Court on February&nbsp;24, 2009.&#160; Amendments to the DIP Credit Agreement were
entered into on February&nbsp;25 and 27, 2009.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The DIP Credit Agreement, as amended, provided for borrowings up to an
aggregate committed amount of $750 million, consisting of a $400 million U.S.
DIP Term Loan for borrowings by the Company; a $35 million Canadian DIP Term
Loan for borrowings by SSC Canada; a $250 million U.S. DIP Revolver for
borrowings by the Company and/or SSC Canada; and a $65 million Canadian DIP
Revolver for borrowings by the Company and/or SSC Canada.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The use of proceeds under the DIP Credit Agreement was limited to (i)&nbsp;working
capital, letters of credit and capital expenditures; (ii)&nbsp;other general
corporate purposes of the Company and certain of its subsidiaries (including
certain intercompany loans); (iii)&nbsp;the refinancing in full of indebtedness
outstanding under the receivables securitization programs; (iv)&nbsp;payment of
any related transaction costs, fees and expenses; and (v)&nbsp;the costs of
administration of the cases arising out of the Chapter 11 Petition and the
Canadian Petition.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Under the DIP Credit Agreement, on January&nbsp;28,
2009, the Company borrowed $440 million, consisting of a $400 million U.S. DIP
Term Loan, a $35 million Canadian DIP Term loan and $5 million from the
Canadian DIP Revolver.&#160; In accordance with the
terms of the DIP Credit Agreement, in January&nbsp;2009 the Company used U.S.
DIP Term Loan proceeds of $360 million, net of lenders fees of $40 million, and
Canadian DIP Term Loan proceeds of $30 million, net of lenders fees of $5
million, to terminate the receivables securitization programs and repay all
indebtedness outstanding under the programs of $385 million and to pay other
expenses of $1 million.&#160; In addition,
other fees and expenses of $17 million related to the DIP Credit Agreement were
paid for with proceeds of $5 million from the Canadian DIP Revolver and
available cash.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">During 2009, the Company made
voluntary prepayments of approximately $383 million on the $400 million U.S.
DIP Term Loan with available cash provided by operating activities.&#160; In addition, during 2009, the Company repaid
$17 million of the U.S. DIP Term Loan with proceeds from property sales. &#160;As of December&nbsp;31, 2009, no borrowings
were outstanding under the U.S. DIP Term Loan or the U.S. DIP Revolver.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">During 2009, the Company repaid $35
million on the Canadian DIP Term Loan primarily with proceeds from property

the Company repaid $5 million on the Canadian DIP Revolver. As of December&nbsp;31,

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In March&nbsp;2007, the Company
completed an offering of $675 million of 8.00% unsecured senior notes due March&nbsp;15,
2017.&#160; The Company used the proceeds of
this issuance to repay $546 million of the 9.75% unsecured senior notes due
2011, which were purchased in connection with a cash tender offer, pay related
tender premiums and accrued interest of $19 million and $8 million,
respectively, and repay $95 million of the Company&#146;s revolving credit
facility.&#160; In addition, the Company used
the proceeds to pay fees and expenses of $7 million related to this
transaction.&#160; A loss on early
extinguishment of debt of $23 million was recorded in the first quarter of
2007, including $19 million for tender premiums and a $4 million write-off of
unamortized deferred debt issuance costs.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In May&nbsp;2007, the Company
redeemed the remaining $102 million of the 9.75% Senior Notes at a redemption
price of 103.25% plus accrued interest.&#160;
Borrowings under the Company&#146;s revolving credit facility were used to
redeem the notes and pay related call premiums and accrued interest.&#160; A loss on early extinguishment of debt of $5
million was recorded in the second quarter of 2007, including $4 million for
tender premiums and a $1 million write-off of unamortized deferred debt
issuance costs.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Other</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Interest costs capitalized on
construction projects in 2009, 2008 and 2007 totaled $9 million, $17 million
and $10 million, respectively.&#160; Interest
payments on all debt instruments for 2009, 2008 and 2007 were $103 million,
$259 million and $302 million, respectively.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">10.&#160; Derivative Instruments and
Hedging Activities</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On January&nbsp;26,
2009, the Chapter 11 Petition and the Canadian Petition effectively terminated
all existing derivative instruments.&#160;
Termination fair values were calculated based on the potential
settlement value.&#160; During 2009, a letter
of credit in the amount of $18 million was drawn on related to the settlement
of certain commodity derivative instruments (See Note 9).&#160; Excluding these settled liabilities, the
Company&#146;s termination value related to its remaining derivative liabilities was
approximately $60 million, recorded in other current liabilities in the
consolidated balance sheet at December&nbsp;31, 2009.&#160; These derivative liabilities were stayed due
to the filing of the Chapter 11 Petition and the Canadian Petition, at which
time, these liabilities were adjusted through OCI for derivative instruments
qualifying for hedge accounting and cost of goods sold for derivative
instruments not qualifying for hedge accounting.&#160; Subsequently, the amounts adjusted through
OCI were recorded in earnings during 2009 when the underlying transaction was
recognized or when the underlying transaction was no longer expected to occur,
except for a $1 million loss (net of tax) which remained in OCI at December&nbsp;31,
2009.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company&#146;s
derivative instruments previously used for its hedging activities were designed
as cash flow hedges and related to minimizing exposures to fluctuations in the
price of commodities used in its operations, the movement in foreign currency
exchange rates and the fluctuations in the interest rate on variable rate
debt.&#160; All cash flows associated with the
Company&#146;s derivative instruments were classified as operating activities in the
consolidated statements of cash flows.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Commodity Derivative Instruments</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company used derivative
instruments, including fixed price swaps, to manage fluctuations in cash flows
resulting from commodity price risk in the procurement of natural gas and other
commodities, including fuel oil and diesel fuel.&#160; The objective was to fix the price of a
portion of the Company&#146;s purchases of these commodities used in the
manufacturing process.&#160; The changes in
the market value of such derivative instruments historically offset the changes
in the price of the hedged item.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">For the years ended December&nbsp;31,
2009 and 2008, the Company reclassified a $27 million loss (net of tax) and an
$8 million loss (net of tax), respectively, from OCI to cost of goods sold when
the hedged items were recognized.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">For the years ended December&nbsp;31,
2009 and 2008, the Company recorded a $3 million gain (net of tax), prior to
the Petition Date, and an $8 million loss (net of tax), respectively, in cost
of goods sold related to the change in fair value of certain commodity
derivative instruments not qualifying for hedge accounting.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">For the years ended December&nbsp;31,
2009 and 2008, the Company recorded a $3 million loss (net of tax), prior to
the Petition Date, and a $9 million loss (net of tax), respectively, in cost of
goods sold on settled commodity derivative instruments not qualifying for hedge
accounting.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Foreign Currency Derivative
Instruments</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company&#146;s principal foreign
exchange exposure is the Canadian dollar.&#160;
The Company used foreign currency derivative instruments, including
forward contracts and options, primarily to protect against Canadian currency
exchange risk associated with expected future cash flows.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">For the years ended December&nbsp;31,
2009 and 2008, the Company reclassified a $4 million loss (net of tax) and a $2
million gain (net of tax), respectively, from OCI to cost of goods sold when
the hedged items were recognized.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">75<a name="PB_75_120505_7906"></a></font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In addition, during the second
quarter 2009, the Company reclassified the remaining foreign currency
derivative instruments from OCI to cost of goods sold since the underlying
transactions were no longer expected to occur, resulting in a loss of $2
million (net of tax).</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Interest Rate Swap Contracts</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company used interest rate swap
contracts to manage interest rate exposure on $300 million of the current
Tranche B and Tranche C floating rate bank term debt.&#160; The accounting for the cash flow impact of
the swap contracts is recorded as an adjustment to interest expense each
period.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">For the years ended December&nbsp;31,
2009 and 2008, the Company reclassified a $4 million loss (net of tax) and a $2
million loss (net of tax), respectively, from OCI to interest expense when the
hedged items were recognized.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">During the fourth quarter of 2008,
the Company expected that its Tranche B and Tranche C term loans would be
refinanced prior to their current maturity.&#160;
As a result, a portion of the interest rate swap contracts were deemed
to be ineffective and were marked-to-market, resulting in $12 million of
additional interest expense.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Deferred Hedge Gain (Loss)</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The cumulative deferred hedge loss
in OCI on all derivative instruments was $1 million (net of tax) at December&nbsp;31,
2009, consisting of a $1 million loss (net of tax) on interest rate swap
contracts.&#160; The cumulative deferred hedge
loss in OCI on all derivative instruments was $37 million (net of tax) at December&nbsp;31,
2008, including a $26 million loss (net of tax) on commodity derivative
instruments, a $6 million loss (net of tax) on foreign currency derivative
instruments and a $5 million loss (net of tax) on interest rate swap
contracts.&#160; The Company expects to
reclassify the remaining $1 million loss (net of tax) into interest expense
during 2010 related to the interest rate swap contracts.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">12.&#160; Guarantees and Commitments</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company has certain wood chip
processing contracts extending from 2012 through 2018 with minimum purchase
commitments.&#160; As part of the agreements,
the Company guarantees the third party contractor&#146;s debt outstanding and has a
security interest in the chipping equipment.&#160;
At December&nbsp;31, 2009 and 2008, the maximum potential amount of
future payments related to these guarantees was approximately $25 million and
$28 million, respectively, and decreases ratably over the life of the
contracts.&#160; In the event the guarantees
on these contracts were called, proceeds from the liquidation of the chipping
equipment would be based on current market conditions and the Company may not
recover in full the guarantee payments made.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The
Company was contingently liable for $18 million under a one year letter of
credit, which was to expire in April&nbsp;2009, which supported the borrowings
of a previously non-consolidated affiliate.&#160;
On March&nbsp;4, 2009, this letter of credit was drawn on, which
increased borrowings under the Company&#146;s pre-petition credit facilities by $18
million (See Note 9).&#160; As a result of
providing substantial financial support for the affiliate, in accordance with
ASC 810-10-05, &#147;Consolidation of Variable Interest Entities,&#148; the Company
consolidated the affiliate&#146;s balance sheet and results of operations into its
consolidated financial statements in March&nbsp;2009.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">At December&nbsp;31, 2009, the
Company had $706 million of net operating loss (&#147;NOL&#148;) carryforwards for U.S.
federal income tax purposes that expire from 2024 through 2029, with a tax
value of $247 million.&#160; The Company had
NOL carryforwards for state purposes which expire from 2009 to 2028 with a tax
value of $81 million and state tax credits that expire from 2009 to 2039, with
a tax value of $4 million.&#160; Further, the
Company had $396 million of NOL carryforwards for Canadian tax purposes that
expire from 2017 to 2029, with a tax value of $115 million, and Canadian investment
tax credits that expire from 2015 to 2018, with a tax value of $15
million.&#160; The Company had $68 million of
alternative minimum tax credit carryforwards for U.S. federal income tax
purposes, which are available indefinitely.&#160;
In addition, the Company had other tax carryforwards of $2 million at December&nbsp;31,
2009, which can be carried forward indefinitely.&#160; Deferred income taxes related to NOL
carryforwards have been classified as noncurrent to reflect the expected
utilization of the carryforwards.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">At December&nbsp;31, 2009 and 2008,
the Company had a valuation allowance of $382 million and $42 million,
respectively, for a portion of the deferred tax assets.&#160; The valuation allowance increased during 2009
primarily to offset higher deferred tax assets related to tax losses on the
Company&#146;s investment in its Canadian subsidiary.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Federal income taxes have not been
provided on undistributed earnings of the Company&#146;s foreign subsidiaries during
2009, as the Company intends to indefinitely reinvest such earnings into its
foreign subsidiaries.</font><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#160; </font><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The restrictions on remittance of
these earnings, pursuant to the Company&#146;s bankruptcy status, make it not
practicable to determine the amount of the unrecognized deferred tax liability
on these undistributed foreign earnings.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">For the years ended December&nbsp;31,
2009, 2008 and 2007, $3 million, $6 million and $11 million, respectively, of
interest was recorded related to tax positions taken during the current and
prior years.&#160; During 2008, $12 million of
interest was released due to settlements with taxing authorities.&#160; The interest was computed on the difference
between the tax position recognized in accordance with ASC 740 and the amount
previously taken or expected to be taken in the Company&#146;s tax returns, adjusted
to reflect the impact of net operating loss and other tax carryforward
items.&#160; During 2009, no penalties were
recorded related to current and prior year tax positions.&#160; During 2008, $3 million of penalties were
recorded related to these tax positions.&#160;
At December&nbsp;31, 2009 and 2008, $25 million and $22 million,
respectively, of interest and penalties are recognized in the consolidated
balance sheet.&#160; All net unrecognized tax
benefits, if recognized, would affect the Company&#146;s effective tax rate.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">As previously disclosed, the Canada
Revenue Agency (&#147;CRA&#148;) is continuing its examination of the Company&#146;s income
tax returns for tax years 1999 through 2005.&#160;
In connection with the examination, the CRA has issued assessments of
additional income taxes, interest and penalties related to transfer prices of
inventory sold by the Company&#146;s Canadian subsidiaries to its U.S.
subsidiaries.&#160; Additionally, the CRA is
considering certain significant adjustments related principally to taxable
income related to the Company&#146;s acquisition of a Canadian company.&#160; The Company has appealed the assessments related
to the transfer pricing matter.&#160; In order
to appeal the assessment, the Company made payments totaling $25 million to the
CRA in 2008.&#160; The remaining matters may
be resolved at the examination level or subsequently upon appeal within the
next twelve months.&#160; While the final
outcome of the remaining CRA examination matters, including an estimate of the
range of the reasonably possible changes to unrecognized tax benefits, is not
yet determinable, the Company believes that the examination or subsequent appeals
will not have a material adverse effect on its consolidated financial condition
or results of operations.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The U.S. federal statute of
limitations is closed through 2005, except for any potential correlative
adjustments for the years 1999 through 2005 relating to the CRA examinations
noted above.&#160; There are currently no
federal examinations in progress.&#160; In
addition, the Company files tax returns in numerous states.&#160; The states&#146; statutes of limitations are
generally open for the same years as the federal statute of limitations.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company made income tax payments
of $12 million, $55 million and $17 million in 2009, 2008 and 2007,
respectively.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">15.&#160; Employee Benefit Plans</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Defined Benefit Plans</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company sponsors noncontributory
defined benefit pension plans for its U.S. employees and also sponsors
noncontributory and contributory defined benefit pension plans for its Canadian
employees.&#160; The Company&#146;s defined benefit
pension plans cover substantially all hourly employees, as well as salaried
employees hired prior to January&nbsp;1, 2006.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On August&nbsp;31, 2007, the Company
announced the freeze of its defined benefit pension plans for salaried
employees.&#160; The U.S. and Canadian defined
benefit pension plans for salaried employees were frozen effective January&nbsp;1,
2009 and March&nbsp;1, 2009, respectively.&#160;
In accordance with ASC 715, &#147;Compensation-Retirement Benefits,&#148; the Company
accounted for this freeze as a plan curtailment, remeasured its assets and
obligation as of August&nbsp;31, 2007 and recognized a curtailment gain of $3
million during the third quarter of 2007.&#160;
Upon remeasurement, the Company reduced its benefit obligation in other
long-term liabilities by $106 million, decreased accumulated other
comprehensive loss by $64 million and increased deferred income tax liability
by $42 million.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">At December&nbsp;31, 2009, no SSCC
common stock shares were included in the U.S. plan assets. Equity securities
for the U.S. plans at December&nbsp;31, 2008 included 2.7 million shares of
SSCC common stock with a market value of $1 million (less than 1% of total U.S.
plan assets).</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The primary objective of the Company&#146;s
investment policy is to provide eligible employees with scheduled pension
benefits.&#160; The basic strategy of this
investment policy is to earn the highest risk adjusted rate of return on assets
consistent with prudent investor standards identified in the Employee
Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 for the U.S. plans and the Quebec
Supplemental Pension Plans Act and other applicable legislation in Canada for
the Canadian plans.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The fair value of plan assets is
based on a hierarchy of inputs, both observable and unobservable, as follows:</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;"><i><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">Level 1</font></i><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;"> &#150; Valuations based on quoted prices
in active markets for identical assets or liabilities that the Company has the
ability to access.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;"><i><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">Level 2</font></i><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;"> &#150; Valuations based on quoted prices
in markets that are not active or for which all significant inputs are
observable, either directly or indirectly.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;"><i><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">Level 3</font></i><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;"> &#150; Valuations based on inputs that
are unobservable and significant to the overall fair value measurement. </font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;text-indent:-.25in;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">(a)</font><font size="1" face="Arial" style="font-size:8.5pt;">&#160;&#160; </font><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Comprised
primarily of investment grade U.S. and Canadian corporate debt issues.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;text-indent:-.25in;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">(b)</font><font size="1" face="Arial" style="font-size:8.5pt;">&#160;&#160; </font><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Comprised
primarily of diversified U.S. equity securities held in both separate accounts
and common/collective trust funds.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;text-indent:-.25in;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">(c)</font><font size="1" face="Arial" style="font-size:8.5pt;">&#160;&#160; </font><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Comprised
primarily of diversified international equity securities held in both separate
accounts and common/collective trust funds.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">Cash equivalents and Corporate
and Government debt securities</font></i></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Certain investments in government
fixed income securities are valued at the closing price reported on the major
market on which the individual security is traded on and classified within
Level 1 of the valuation hierarchy. The remaining investments in fixed income
securities are valued by third-party pricing services using credit risk spreads
determined from the new issue market and dealer quotes, which is then added to
the U.S. treasury curve.&#160; Such
investments are classified within Level 2 of the valuation hierarchy.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">Common stocks and
Common/collective trusts</font></i></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Common stocks are valued at the
closing price reported on the major market on which the individual securities
are traded. Such investments are classified within Level 1 of the valuation
hierarchy.&#160; Common/collective trusts are
valued using the net asset value (&#147;NAV&#148;) provided by the administrator of the
fund. The NAV is based on the value of the underlying assets owned by the fund,
minus its liabilities, and then divided by the number of shares outstanding.
The NAV is a quoted price in a market that is not active and classified within
Level 2 of the valuation hierarchy.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">Private Equity</font></i></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Private equity is valued by deriving
the Company pension plans&#146; proportionate share of equity investment from
audited financial statements from the previous calendar year updated with
changes in value, withdrawals and contributions for the current year.&#160; These investments primarily consist of
private equity investments that require significant judgment on the part of the
general partner due to the absence of quoted market prices, inherent lack of
liquidity, and the long-term nature of such investments. Such investments are
classified within Level 3 of the valuation hierarchy.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In identifying the target asset
allocation that would best meet the Company&#146;s investment policy, consideration
is given to a number of factors including the various pension plans&#146;
demographic characteristics, the long-term nature of the liabilities, the
sensitivity of the liabilities to interest rates and inflation, the long-term
return expectations and risks associated with key asset classes as well as
their return correlation with each other, diversification among asset classes
and other practical considerations for investing in certain asset classes.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The target asset allocation for the
pension plans during a complete market cycle is as follows:</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<table border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" width="100%" style="border-collapse:collapse;width:100.0%;">
 <tr>
  <td width="66%" valign="bottom" style="padding:0in 0in 0in 0in;width:66.0%;">
  <p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:1.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
  </td>
  <td width="2%" valign="bottom" style="padding:0in 0in 0in 0in;width:2.5%;">
  <p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:1.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
  </td>
  <td width="12%" valign="bottom" style="border:none;border-bottom:solid windowtext 1.0pt;padding:0in 0in 0in 0in;width:12.0%;">

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Postretirement Health Care and Life Insurance Benefits</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company provides certain health
care and life insurance benefits for all retired salaried and certain retired
hourly employees, and for salaried and certain hourly employees who reached the
age of 60 with ten years of service as of January&nbsp;1, 2007.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The effect of a 1% change in the
assumed health care cost trend rate would increase and decrease the APBO as of December&nbsp;31,
2009 by $10 million and $9 million, respectively, and would increase and
decrease the annual net periodic postretirement benefit cost for 2009 by $1
million and $1 million, respectively.</font></p>

2009 and 2008, respectively.</font></p>

accumulated benefit obligation and fair value of plan assets for the pension
plans with accumulated benefit obligations in excess of plan assets were $3,564
million, $3,516 million and $2,434 million, respectively, as of December&nbsp;31,
2009 and $3,103 million, $3,076 million, and $2,100 million, respectively, as
of December&nbsp;31, 2008.</font></p>

respectively, as of December&nbsp;31, 2009 and $3,190 million and $2,183
million, respectively, as of December&nbsp;31, 2008.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In 2007, closed facilities resulted
in a $3 million curtailment loss related to the defined benefit plans and a $3
million curtailment gain related to the postretirement plans.&#160; The salaried defined benefit plan freeze,
resulting in a $3 million gain, offset the impact of the closed facilities.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The settlement losses in each year
and the 2008 and 2009 curtailment (gains) losses are related to closed
facilities and are included as part of restructuring charges (See Note 3).</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The fundamental assumptions behind
the expected rate of return are the cumulative effect of several estimates,
including the anticipated yield on high quality debt securities, the equity
risk premium earned by investing in equity securities over a long-term time
horizon and active investment management.&#160;
Based on adjustments to the future target asset allocation, effective January&nbsp;1,
2010, the expected long-term rate of return for the Canadian plans is 6.30%.</font></p>

  <p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:1.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
  </td>
  <td width="1%" valign="bottom" style="padding:0in 0in 0in 0in;width:1.16%;">
  <p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:1.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
  </td>
 </tr>
</table>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Savings Plans</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company sponsors savings plans covering
substantially all salaried and certain hourly employees.&#160; The Company match is invested according to
the employees&#146; selected investment allocation.&#160;
Effective January&nbsp;1, 2009 for the salaried plan, the Company
contributes an additional amount equal to 1% of each eligible employee&#146;s
salary.&#160; In addition, the matching
formula for the salaried plan was changed from 70% of the first 6% of an
employee&#146;s deferral to 100% of the first 6% of an employee&#146;s deferral.&#160; The Company&#146;s expense for the savings plans
totaled $25 million, $17 million and $18 million in 2009, 2008 and 2007,
respectively.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">16.&#160; Stock&#151;Based Compensation</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">SSCC has stock options and RSUs
outstanding under several long-term incentive plans. The stock options and RSUs
have been granted primarily to certain employees of the Company.&#160; The 1998 Long-Term Incentive Plan (the &#147;1998
Plan&#148;) and the 2004 Long-Term Incentive Plan (the &#147;2004 Plan&#148;) have reserved
16.5 million and 12.5 million shares, respectively, of SSCC common stock for
non-qualified stock options, RSUs and performance-based stock options to
officers, key employees and non-employee directors of the Company.&#160; The stock options are exercisable at a price
equal to the fair market value of SSCC&#146;s stock on the date of grant.&#160; The vesting schedule and other terms and
conditions of options granted under each plan are established separately for
each grant.&#160; The options expire no later
than seven to ten years from the date of grant.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Certain grants under the 1998 Plan
and the 2004 Plan contain change in control provisions which provide for
immediate vesting and exercisability in the event that specific ownership
conditions are met.&#160; Grants issued before
December&nbsp;31, 2005 allowed for immediate vesting and exercisability in the
event of retirement.&#160; For grants issued
after December&nbsp;31, 2005, unvested awards do not vest upon retirement.&#160; Vested options remain exercisable until the
earlier of five years from retirement or ten years from the initial grant date.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company uses a lattice option
pricing model to estimate the fair value of stock options as it more fully
reflects the substantive characteristics of the Company&#146;s stock-based
compensation.&#160; The lattice option pricing
model considers a range of assumptions related to volatility, risk-free interest
rate and historical employee behavior.&#160;
Expected volatility was based on historical volatility on SSCC common
stock and current implied volatilities from traded options on SSCC common
stock.&#160; The risk-free interest rate was
based on U.S. Treasury security yields at the time of grant.&#160; The dividend yield on SSCC common stock is
assumed to be zero since SSCC has not paid dividends and has no current plans
to do so in the future.&#160; The expected
life was determined from the lattice option pricing model.&#160; The lattice option pricing model incorporates
exercise and post-vesting forfeiture assumptions based on analysis of
historical data.</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Total pretax
stock-based compensation costs recognized in selling and administrative
expenses in the consolidated statements of operations for 2009, 2008 and 2007
were $9 million, $3 million and $21 million, respectively.&#160; The related tax benefit for 2009, 2008 and
2007 was $3 million, $1 million and $8 million, respectively.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">During 2008,
the Company reversed stock compensation expense of $13 million related to
performance-based stock options granted in 2006 and 2007 as the vesting
requirements were no longer attainable.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">At December&nbsp;31,
2009, the total compensation cost related to non-vested awards not yet
recognized was approximately $5 million to be recognized through December&nbsp;31,
2011, with a weighted-average expense period of approximately 1 year.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Stock Options</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Grants issued subsequent to June&nbsp;2004
vest and become exercisable on the third anniversary of the award date.&#160; The stock options granted prior to January&nbsp;2007
are fully vested and exercisable.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">RSUs</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Through December&nbsp;31, 2008, the
Company issued SSCC RSUs to pay a portion of employee bonuses under its annual
management incentive plan.&#160; These RSUs
vest immediately, but are not distributed to active employees until the third
anniversary of the award date.&#160; Through December&nbsp;31,
2008, the Company paid a premium on the employee bonuses in the form of SSCC
RSUs (&#147;Premium RSUs&#148;) to certain employees.&#160;
The Company also issued non-vested SSCC RSUs under the 2004 Plan to
certain employees.&#160; Non-employee
directors were also annually awarded non-vested SSCC RSUs as part of their
director compensation.&#160; These non-vested
RSUs and Premium RSUs vest at the earlier of a change in control, death,
disability or three years after the award date.&#160;
The SSCC RSUs are non-transferable and do not have voting rights.&#160; There were no RSU&#146;s issued during 2009.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">18.&#160; Goodwill and Other Intangible
Assets</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company evaluates goodwill and other intangible assets
for impairment in accordance with ASC 350, &#147;Intangibles - Goodwill and Other&#148; (&#147;ASC
350&#148;), annually or at other times when events and circumstances indicate the
carrying value of this asset may no longer be fully recoverable.&#160; In the fourth quarter of 2008, as the result
of the significant decline in value of SSCC equity securities and the Company&#146;s
debt instruments and the downward pressure placed on earnings by the weakening
U.S. economy, the Company determined that goodwill and other intangible assets
were potentially impaired.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<h1 style="font-weight:bold;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;page-break-after:avoid;"><b><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:normal;">The
Company engaged a third-party to assist with its impairment review.&#160; As outlined in ASC 350, the amount of the
goodwill impairment, if any, is measured by comparing the implied fair value of
goodwill to its book value, or carrying amount.&#160;
The third-party valuation report as of December&nbsp;31, 2008, indicated
that the carrying amount of goodwill was fully impaired based on declines in
current and projected operating results and cash flows due the current economic
conditions.&#160; At December&nbsp;31, 2008,
the Company recognized an impairment charge of $2,723 million, net of an income
tax benefit of $4 million, which eliminated all goodwill.&#160;&#160; The goodwill consisted primarily of amounts
recorded in connection with the Company&#146;s merger with Stone Container
Corporation in November&nbsp;1998.</font></b></h1>

Smurfit-MBI in 2003.&#160; As a result, the
Company recognized a pretax impairment charge on other intangible assets of $34
million in the fourth quarter of 2008.</font></p>

and intangible asset balances were zero at December&nbsp;31, 2009 and December&nbsp;31,

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">20.&#160; Fair Value Measurements</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Certain financial assets and
liabilities are recorded at fair value on a recurring basis, including
derivative instruments prior to termination (See Note 10), the Company&#146;s
retained interest in receivables sold to the accounts receivable programs (See
Note 8) prior to termination of these programs on January&nbsp;28, 2009 and the
Company&#146;s residual interest in TNH (See Note 8).</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Fair value is defined as the price
that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an
orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date.&#160; In determining fair value, the Company uses
various valuation approaches, including market, income and/or cost
approaches.&#160; ASC 820, &#147;Fair Value
Measurements and Disclosures,&#148; establishes a hierarchy for inputs used in
measuring fair value that maximizes the use of observable inputs and minimizes
the use of unobservable inputs by requiring that the most observable inputs be
used when available.&#160; Observable inputs
are inputs that market participants would use in pricing the asset or liability
based on market data obtained from sources independent of the Company.&#160; Unobservable inputs are inputs that reflect
the Company&#146;s assumptions about the assumptions market participants would use
in pricing the asset or liability developed based on the best information
available in the circumstances.&#160; The
hierarchy for inputs is broken down into three levels based on their
reliability as follows:</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;"><i><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">Level 1</font></i><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;"> &#151; Valuations based on quoted prices
in active markets for identical assets or liabilities that the Company has the ability
to access.&#160; The Company has no assets or
liabilities measured at fair value on a recurring basis utilizing Level 1
inputs.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;"><i><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">Level 2</font></i><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;"> &#151; Valuations based on quoted prices
in markets that are not active or for which all significant inputs are
observable, either directly or indirectly.&#160;
The Company has no assets or liabilities measured at fair value on a
recurring basis utilizing Level 2 inputs.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;"><i><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">Level 3</font></i><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;"> &#151; Valuations based on inputs that
are unobservable and significant to the overall fair value measurement.&#160; The Company&#146;s assets and liabilities
utilizing Level 3 inputs include the residual interest in the TNH
investment.&#160; The fair value of the
residual interest in the TNH investment is estimated using discounted residual
cash flows.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Fair Value on a Recurring Basis</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Assets and liabilities measured at
fair value on a recurring basis are categorized in the table below based upon
the level of input to the valuations.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="left" style="letter-spacing:-.1pt;line-height:normal;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;letter-spacing:0pt;">Unrealized gains (losses) associated with derivative instruments represent
the change in fair value included in OCI for derivative instruments qualifying
for hedge accounting and cost of goods sold for derivative instruments not
qualifying for hedge accounting (See Note 10).</font></p>

<p align="left" style="letter-spacing:-.1pt;line-height:normal;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;letter-spacing:0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="left" style="letter-spacing:-.1pt;line-height:normal;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;letter-spacing:0pt;">The net settlements associated with retained interest in receivables sold
are due to the termination of the securitization programs (See Note 8).&#160; The net payments associated with derivative
instruments relate to pre-bankruptcy filing contract settlements and the
settlement of contracts at termination, which were supported by letters of
credits (See Note 9).</font></p>

<p align="left" style="letter-spacing:-.1pt;line-height:normal;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;letter-spacing:0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="left" style="letter-spacing:-.1pt;line-height:normal;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;letter-spacing:0pt;">Due to termination of all existing derivative instruments, these
liabilities are no longer measured at fair value on a recurring basis (See Note
10).</font></p>

<p align="left" style="letter-spacing:-.1pt;line-height:normal;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;letter-spacing:0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="left" style="letter-spacing:-.1pt;line-height:normal;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;"><b><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;letter-spacing:0pt;">Financial Instruments Not Measured At Fair Value</font></b></p>

<p align="left" style="letter-spacing:-.1pt;line-height:normal;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;letter-spacing:0pt;">Some of the Company&#146;s financial instruments are not measured at fair value
on a recurring basis but are recorded at amounts that approximate fair value
due to their liquid or short-term nature.&#160;
The carrying amount of cash equivalents approximates fair value because
of the short maturity of those instruments.&#160;
The fair values of notes receivable are based on discounted future cash
flows or the applicable quoted market price.</font></p>

<p align="left" style="letter-spacing:-.1pt;line-height:normal;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;letter-spacing:0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="left" style="letter-spacing:-.1pt;line-height:normal;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;letter-spacing:0pt;">The Company&#146;s borrowings are recorded at historical amounts.&#160; The fair value of the Company&#146;s debt is
estimated based on the quoted market prices for the same or similar issues or
on the current rates offered to the Company for debt of the same remaining
maturities.&#160; At December&nbsp;31, 2009,
the carrying value and fair value of the Company&#146;s secured borrowings were
$1,354 million and $1,347 million, respectively.&#160; At December&nbsp;31, 2009, the carrying value
and the fair value of the Company&#146;s unsecured borrowings, included in
liabilities subject to compromise, were $2,439 and $2,172, respectively.&#160; At December&nbsp;31, 2008, the carrying value
and fair value of the Company&#146;s borrowings were $3,718 million and $1,678
million, respectively.</font></p>

<p align="left" style="letter-spacing:-.1pt;line-height:normal;margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:left;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;letter-spacing:0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .25in;text-indent:-.25in;"><b><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">22.&#160; Contigencies</font></b></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .25in;text-indent:-.25in;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company&#146;s past and present
operations include activities which are subject to federal, state and local
environmental requirements, particularly relating to air and water
quality.&#160; The Company faces potential
environmental liability as a result of violations of these environmental
requirements, environmental permit terms and similar authorizations that have
occurred from time to time at its facilities.&#160;
In addition, the Company faces potential liability for remediation at
certain owned and formerly owned facilities, as well as response costs at
various sites for which it has received notice as being a potentially
responsible party</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">92<a name="PB_92_015859_8146"></a></font></p>

<div>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;"><a href="#TableOfContents" title="Click to go to Table of Contents">Table of
Contents</a></font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">(&#147;PRP&#148;) concerning hazardous substance
contamination.&#160; In estimating its
reserves for environmental remediation and future costs, the Company&#146;s
estimated liability of $5 million reflects the Company&#146;s expected share of
costs after consideration for the relative percentage of waste deposited at
each site, the number of other PRPs, the identity and financial condition of
such parties and experience regarding similar matters.&#160; As of December&nbsp;31, 2009, the Company had
approximately $28 million reserved for environmental liabilities, of which $14 million
is included in other long-term liabilities and $14 million in other current
liabilities, in the consolidated balance sheets.&#160; The Company believes the liability for these
matters was adequately reserved at December&nbsp;31, 2009.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">If all or most of the other PRPs are
unable to satisfy their portion of the clean-up costs at one or more of the
significant sites in which the Company is involved or the Company&#146;s expected
share increases, the resulting liability could have a material adverse effect
on the Company&#146;s consolidated financial condition, results of operations or
cash flows.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In January&nbsp;2009, the Company
settled two putative class action cases filed in California state court on
behalf of current and former hourly employees at the Company&#146;s California
corrugated container facilities.&#160; These
cases alleged violations of the California on-duty meal break and rest period
statutes.&#160; The court approved a
settlement for a total of $9 million for both cases on January&nbsp;21,
2009.&#160; The cases were automatically stayed
due to the filing of the Chapter 11 Petition on January&nbsp;26, 2009 (See Note
1).&#160; The Company established reserves of
$9 million during 2008 related to these matters, which was included in selling
and administrative expenses in the accompanying consolidated statement of
operations.&#160; It is anticipated that the
Company&#146;s liability for the settlement of these cases will be satisfied as an
unsecured claim in the U.S. bankruptcy proceedings.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In May&nbsp;2009, a lawsuit was
filed in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois
against the four individual committee members of the Administrative Committee (&#147;Administrative
Committee&#148;) of the Company&#146;s savings plans and Patrick Moore, the Company&#146;s
Chief Executive Officer (together, the &#147;Defendants&#148;).&#160; The suit alleges violations of the Employee
Retirement Income Security Act (&#147;ERISA&#148;) (the &#147;2009 ERISA Case&#148;) between January&nbsp;2008
and the date it was filed.&#160; The
plaintiffs in the 2009 ERISA Case brought the complaint on behalf of themselves
and a class of similarly situated participants and beneficiaries of four of the
Company&#146;s savings plans (the &#147;Savings Plans&#148;).&#160;
The plaintiffs assert that the Defendants breached their fiduciary
duties to the Savings Plans&#146; participants and beneficiaries by allegedly making
imprudent investments with the Savings Plans&#146; assets, making misrepresentations
and failing to disclose material adverse facts concerning the Company&#146;s
business conditions, debt management and viability, and not taking appropriate
action to protect the Savings Plans&#146; assets.&#160;
Even though the Company is not a named defendant in the 2009 ERISA Case,
management believes that any indemnification obligations to the Defendants
would be covered by applicable insurance.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-autospace:none;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On January&nbsp;11,
2010, a second ERISA class action lawsuit was filed in the United States
District Court for the Western District of Missouri.&#160; The defendants in this case are the
individual committee members of the Administrative Committee, several other of
the Company&#146;s executives and the individual members of its Board of
Directors.&#160; The suit has similar
allegations as the 2009 ERISA Case described above, with the addition of breach
of fiduciary duty claims related to the Company&#146;s pension plans.&#160; The Company expects that both of these
matters will be consolidated in some manner as they purport to represent a
similar class of employees and former employees and seek recovery under similar
allegations and any of the Company&#146;s indemnification obligations would be
covered by applicable insurance.</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Arial" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company is a defendant in a
number of other lawsuits and claims arising out of the conduct of its
business.&#160; All litigation that arose or
may arise out of pre-petition conduct or acts is subject to the automatic stay
provision of the bankruptcy laws and any recovery by plaintiffs in those
matters will be paid consistent with all other general unsecured claims in the
bankruptcy.&#160; As a result, the Company
believes that these matters will not have a material adverse effect on its
consolidated financial condition, results of operations or cash flows.</font></p>
